title: The Knight’s Return
summary: Choose a knight instead of a queen, then trade a material advantage for a winning king-and-pawn position.

nodes.question: How can a knight and pawns overcome a queen?
nodes.explanation: Keep checking while preparing promotion. Black is looking for stalemate, not just material.

nodes.question: Which piece should the pawn become?
nodes.explanation: Promotion changes the defender’s legal moves. Compare a queen with a checking knight.

nodes.question: Should White save the remaining knight?
nodes.explanation: The king can win the pawn ending even if the knight is captured.

branches.title: Follow the underpromotion and king plan
commentary: White must create forcing threats before Black can use the queen. Count the defender’s legal replies, not just the material.
b7+ uses the pawn to check the cornered king and prepares promotion.
Ka7 is forced: the knight and white king cover Black’s other escape squares.
Nc6+ checks again, moving the original knight away from b8.
Ka6 sets the stalemate trap. A queen promotion is no longer the right choice.
b8=N+ promotes with check. The knight attacks a6, so Black cannot immediately spring a queen-sacrifice stalemate.
Kb6 is the only legal answer to the knight check.
Nd7+ brings the promoted knight into play. It checks b6 while the original knight on c6 is offered to the king.
Kxc6 captures the original knight, not the checking knight on d7. This king capture creates the next fork.
Ne5+ checks the king on c6 and attacks the queen on d3.
Kd5 is a legal illustrated reply. The king moves, but the queen remains under attack.
Nxd3 wins the queen. Keep calculating: the extra knight alone does not settle the pawn race.
Kc4 attacks the knight on d3 and the pawn on b4. Saving the knight carelessly can lose the last white pawn.
Kc7 activates the king while leaving the knight to be taken. The pawn ending, rather than the knight, is the winning asset.
Kxd3 takes the knight. White has calculated the resulting king route before giving it up.
Kb6 attacks b5. Black must keep the pawn guarded.
Kc4 guards b5 from its only accessible defending square.
Ka5 keeps the threat against b5 and hands Black the move. The king cannot stay on c4.
Kd5 is one representative retreat; Black has to abandon the pawn’s defense.
Kxb5 wins the pawn and leaves a verified winning king-and-pawn ending. The earlier knight sacrifice enabled this king route.
branches.explanation: Kxb5 wins the pawn and leaves a verified winning king-and-pawn ending. The earlier knight sacrifice enabled this king route.

branches.title: Try the natural queen promotion
commentary: The natural promotion gives the queen maximum power, but it can also remove every black king move.
b8=Q controls the b-file. That restriction will become a problem after Black’s next check.
Qd7+ offers the queen with check. In this position White’s only legal answer is to take it with the king.
Kxd7 leaves Black without a legal move and without being in check: stalemate. The white queen controls b6 and b7, the knight controls a5 and a7, and the b-pawn is blocked.
branches.explanation: Kxd7 leaves Black without a legal move and without being in check: stalemate. The white queen controls b6 and b7, the knight controls a5 and a7, and the b-pawn is blocked.

branches.title: Try saving the knight first
commentary: Black attacks the knight and pawn. Compare saving material with activating the king.
Ne5+ saves the knight with check, but abandons the pawn on b4. This already gives up White’s forced win.
Kxb4 removes White’s last pawn. The tablebase result is a draw; the extra knight does not provide a forced win.
branches.explanation: Kxb4 removes White’s last pawn. The tablebase result is a draw; the extra knight does not provide a forced win.

exercises.prompt: Why is a knight promotion stronger than a queen here?
exercises.answer: The knight promotes with check. The queen permits ...Qd7+ and the forced king capture leaves Black stalemated.

exercises.prompt: What do you need to calculate before Kc7?
exercises.answer: Check the king-and-pawn ending after ...Kxd3: Kb6 attacks b5, ...Kc4 guards it, and Ka5 leaves Black unable to keep defending the pawn.

verification_scope: Selected positions reconstructed from saved source images. Every encoded move and intermediate outcome is checked; representative replies illustrate the idea without enumerating every legal defense.
